primitives.name: Spatial-Temporal Shortcut Preference
primitives.verbatim_quote: Least Effort We have seen that rats prefer spatially shorter and temporally shorter routes, and we have suggested that probably they also can differentiate and prefer gravitationally (i.e., force-resistingly) shorter routes.
primitives.assumptions: Rats optimize both spatial and temporal cost simultaneously.
primitives.breakdown_regime: In complex mazes with conflicting local optima, shortcut preference may fail due to local minima trapping.

The primitives emerge from empirical observations of rat behavior in mazes, where force-resistance, spatial-temporal shortcuts, and least-effort principles interplay. The core idea is that rats' path selection reflects an optimization over multiple dimensions—physical effort, time, and distance. This leads to a unified framework where each primitive represents a facet of a deeper, more general principle. Force resistance preference is foundational, suggesting that rats inherently avoid high-force trajectories. Spatial-temporal shortcut preference builds upon this by extending the concept to include temporal efficiency. The least-effort hypothesis synthesizes these into a single overarching principle. Each primitive is grounded in measurable variables and can be mapped to formal inference and reasoning engines in GSI and GSE respectively. Dualities arise in how these principles interact—e.g., a path may be shorter but require more force, leading to potential conflicts. Failure modes occur when environmental complexity exceeds the predictive capacity of any single model, necessitating layered reasoning.
